title: Farm Runoff and Stream Insects
topic: Aquatic ecosystems · Nutrient pollution and indicator species

modeledOn.label: 2025 AP Environmental Science Set 1 Question 1 (Design an Investigation)

stimulus.content:
Figure 1: Grouped bar graph for Sites 1 to 5. Nitrate in mg per liter: 1, 3, 6, 9, 12. Number of EPT taxa: 14, 11, 7, 4, 2

Figure 2
Site | Dissolved oxygen at dawn (mg/L)
1 | 9.1
2 | 8.0
3 | 6.2
4 | 4.1

prompt: A stream flows past a large corn farm. Mayflies, stoneflies, and caddisflies (EPT insects) are aquatic larvae that are sensitive to pollution. Students sampled five sites at increasing distances downstream from where the farm’s drainage ditch enters the stream. At each site they measured the nitrate concentration and counted the number of different EPT taxa in a standard kick-net sample (Figure 1). They also measured dissolved oxygen at dawn at the same sites (Figure 2).

parts.label: A
parts.text: Describe one ecosystem service that a healthy stream provides to people.

rubricPoints.criterion: Describes a provisioning, regulating, cultural, or supporting service of a stream (for example, water purification, fish for food, flood control, or recreation).
commonErrors: names a service without describing it
describes a farm benefit unrelated to the stream
rubricPoints.exampleEarning: Wetland plants and microbes along the stream filter pollutants, providing cleaner drinking water.

parts.label: B
parts.text: Explain how excess nitrate entering the stream could lead to lower dissolved oxygen.

rubricPoints.criterion: Explains eutrophication: nitrate fuels algal blooms; when the algae die, bacteria decompose them and use up dissolved oxygen.
rubricPoints.exampleEarning: Nitrate causes an algal bloom; decomposers breaking down the dead algae consume dissolved oxygen.

parts.label: C
parts.text: Based on Figure 1, identify the number of EPT taxa at Site 3.

rubricPoints.criterion: Identifies 7 taxa.
rubricPoints.exampleEarning: 7 taxa.

parts.label: D
parts.text: Based on Figure 1, describe the relationship between nitrate concentration and the number of EPT taxa.

rubricPoints.criterion: Describes a negative (inverse) relationship: as nitrate increases, the number of EPT taxa decreases.
rubricPoints.exampleEarning: As nitrate increases from 1 to 12 mg/L, EPT taxa fall from 14 to 2.

parts.label: E
parts.text: EPT larvae generally need at least 5 mg/L of dissolved oxygen. Describe one way the data in Figure 2 support the hypothesis that low oxygen helps explain the loss of EPT taxa.

rubricPoints.criterion: Describes that the sites with the fewest taxa (Sites 4 and 5) have dissolved oxygen below 5 mg/L, while sites with more taxa are above 5 mg/L.
rubricPoints.exampleEarning: Sites 4 and 5 have DO of 4.1 and 2.9 mg/L, below 5 mg/L, and the fewest taxa.

parts.label: F
parts.text: The students plan a follow-up investigation that compares the stream above and below the drainage ditch. (i) Identify a testable scientific question for the investigation. (ii) Identify the dependent variable.

rubricPoints.criterion: Identifies a testable question comparing the two locations, such as whether EPT diversity differs above and below the ditch.
rubricPoints.exampleEarning: Does the number of EPT taxa differ between sites upstream and downstream of the drainage ditch?

rubricPoints.criterion: Identifies the number of EPT taxa (or another measured biotic or water-quality response) as the dependent variable.
rubricPoints.exampleEarning: The number of EPT taxa per sample.

parts.label: G
parts.text: (i) Explain why a stream with many EPT taxa would be more likely to recover from a pollution spill than a stream with few. (ii) Explain how the results could have been different if the students had sampled only during a period of heavy rain.

rubricPoints.criterion: Explains that higher species diversity makes it more likely that some species tolerate or survive the disturbance and repopulate (greater resilience).
commonErrors: says more insects eat the pollution
rubricPoints.exampleEarning: With more species, some are likely to survive the spill and help the community recover.

rubricPoints.criterion: Explains a plausible change, such as heavy rain increasing runoff and nitrate levels, or diluting nitrate and raising oxygen, so measurements would differ from typical conditions.
commonErrors: gives a change without a reason
rubricPoints.exampleEarning: Heavy rain washes more fertilizer into the stream, so nitrate readings would be higher than usual.

parts.label: H
parts.text: Describe one agricultural practice that could reduce nitrate runoff from the farm.

rubricPoints.criterion: Describes a practice such as vegetated buffer strips, cover crops, precision or reduced fertilizer application, or no-till farming, with how it reduces runoff.
commonErrors: names a practice that increases runoff
rubricPoints.exampleEarning: Plant a buffer strip of grasses along the stream to absorb nitrate before it reaches the water.

sampleResponse: A Stream wetlands and microbes filter pollutants, providing cleaner water for people downstream. B Nitrate fertilizes algae, causing a bloom; when the algae die, bacteria decompose them and consume dissolved oxygen. C 7 taxa. D As nitrate increases, the number of EPT taxa decreases (a negative relationship). E Sites 4 and 5 have dissolved oxygen of 4.1 and 2.9 mg/L, below the 5 mg/L EPT larvae need, and they have the fewest taxa. F (i) Does the number of EPT taxa differ upstream and downstream of the drainage ditch? (ii) The number of EPT taxa. G (i) A more diverse community is more likely to contain species that survive a spill and recolonize. (ii) Heavy rain would wash more fertilizer into the stream, raising nitrate above normal levels. H Plant vegetated buffer strips along the stream to absorb nitrate in runoff.

title: Coral Bleaching
topic: Ocean warming, acidification, and reef protection

modeledOn.type: Analyze an Environmental Problem and Propose a Solution
modeledOn.label: 2025 AP Environmental Science Set 1 Question 2 (Analyze an Environmental Problem and Propose a Solution)

stimulus.content:
Figure 1
Survey year | Average summer sea temperature (°C) | Bleached colonies (%)
2010 | 28.6 | 5
2013 | 28.9 | 8
2016 | 30.1 | 30
2019 | 29.7 | 22
2022 | 30.6 | 45

prompt: Coral reefs are built by coral animals that host photosynthetic algae called zooxanthellae. Figure 1 gives the average summer sea surface temperature at a reef and the percent of coral colonies that were bleached in each survey year.

figures.caption: Figure 1
figures.alt: Figure 1: Survey year 2010, Average summer sea temperature (°C) 28.6, Bleached colonies (%) 5; Survey year 2013, Average summer sea temperature (°C) 28.9, Bleached colonies (%) 8; Survey year 2016, Average summer sea temperature (°C) 30.1, Bleached colonies (%) 30; Survey year 2019, Average summer sea temperature (°C) 29.7, Bleached colonies (%) 22; Survey year 2022, Average summer sea temperature (°C) 30.6, Bleached colonies (%) 45

parts.label: A
parts.text: Identify the type of relationship between corals and zooxanthellae.

rubricPoints.criterion: Identifies mutualism.
rubricPoints.exampleEarning: Mutualism.

parts.label: B
parts.text: Describe what happens during coral bleaching.

rubricPoints.criterion: Describes stressed corals expelling their zooxanthellae, losing color and their main food source.
commonErrors: says the coral is painted white by sediment
rubricPoints.exampleEarning: Under heat stress, corals expel their algae, turn white, and lose most of their food supply.

parts.label: C
parts.text: Based on Figure 1, identify the year with the highest percent of bleached colonies and describe the relationship between temperature and bleaching.

rubricPoints.criterion: Identifies 2022 and describes that years with higher temperatures had more bleaching (positive relationship).
rubricPoints.exampleEarning: 2022; bleaching rises as sea temperature rises.

parts.label: D
parts.text: Explain how increased atmospheric carbon dioxide can harm coral reefs other than by warming the water.

rubricPoints.criterion: Explains ocean acidification: CO₂ dissolves to form carbonic acid, lowering pH and carbonate availability, which makes it harder for corals to build calcium carbonate skeletons.
rubricPoints.exampleEarning: CO₂ forms carbonic acid in seawater, lowering pH and reducing the carbonate corals need to build skeletons.

parts.label: E
parts.text: Propose a realistic solution a coastal community could implement to reduce a local stress on coral reefs.

rubricPoints.criterion: Proposes a realistic local action, such as establishing a marine protected area, reducing sewage or fertilizer runoff, limiting destructive fishing, or regulating anchoring and tourism.
commonErrors: proposes an unrealistic action such as cooling the ocean
rubricPoints.exampleEarning: Create a marine protected area that bans fishing and anchoring on the reef.

parts.label: F
parts.text: Justify the solution in part E by describing an additional benefit other than protecting corals.

rubricPoints.criterion: Describes an additional benefit consistent with part E (for example, fish populations rebound and support nearby fisheries, ecotourism income, or cleaner water for swimming).
rubricPoints.exampleEarning: Fish populations grow inside the reserve and spill over into fished areas, supporting local fishers.

parts.label: G
parts.text: Describe one ecosystem service provided by coral reefs.

rubricPoints.criterion: Describes a service such as protecting shorelines from wave erosion, providing fish habitat, supporting tourism, or supplying compounds for medicine.
commonErrors: names a service without describing it
rubricPoints.exampleEarning: Reefs break waves and protect coastlines from erosion during storms.

parts.label: H
parts.text: Identify one human activity, other than burning fossil fuels, that damages coral reefs.

rubricPoints.criterion: Identifies a valid activity such as blast or cyanide fishing, sedimentation from coastal development, nutrient runoff, or anchor damage.
commonErrors: identifies a global stress already excluded
rubricPoints.exampleEarning: Sediment from coastal construction smothering the reef.

parts.label: I
parts.text: Describe how the loss of a coral reef could affect a nearby fishing community.

rubricPoints.criterion: Describes that losing reef habitat reduces fish populations, lowering catches, income, or food supply for the community.
rubricPoints.exampleEarning: Fewer reef fish would mean smaller catches and less income for fishers.

parts.label: J
parts.text: Describe one international or national approach to reducing the global cause of rising sea temperatures.

rubricPoints.criterion: Describes an approach to reducing greenhouse gas emissions, such as an international agreement with emissions targets, a carbon tax, or cap-and-trade.
rubricPoints.exampleEarning: A carbon tax that makes fossil fuels more expensive and lowers CO₂ emissions.

sampleResponse: A Mutualism. B Heat-stressed corals expel their zooxanthellae, turning white and losing their main food source. C 2022; bleaching is higher in years with higher sea temperatures. D CO₂ dissolves in seawater to form carbonic acid, lowering pH and reducing the carbonate ions corals need to build calcium carbonate skeletons. E Establish a marine protected area that bans fishing and anchoring on the reef. F Fish populations recover inside the reserve and spill over into nearby waters, supporting local fishers. G Reefs absorb wave energy and protect coastlines from erosion. H Sediment runoff from coastal construction. I Losing the reef would reduce fish habitat and catches, lowering fishers’ income and food supply. J A carbon tax that raises the price of fossil fuels and reduces CO₂ emissions.

title: Rooftop Solar for a Household
topic: Energy resources, air pollution, and calculations

modeledOn.type: Analyze an Environmental Problem and Propose a Solution (Doing Calculations)
modeledOn.label: 2025 AP Environmental Science Set 1 Question 3 (Analyze an Environmental Problem and Propose a Solution (Doing Calculations))

prompt: A household uses 10,800 kWh of electricity per year, all supplied by a coal-fired power plant. The plant releases 1.0 kg of CO₂ for each kWh generated. The household installs rooftop solar panels that cost $18,900 and generate 7,560 kWh per year. Electricity from the utility costs $0.14 per kWh.

parts.label: A
parts.text: Identify one air pollutant, other than carbon dioxide, released by burning coal.

rubricPoints.criterion: Identifies sulfur dioxide, nitrogen oxides, particulate matter, or mercury.
commonErrors: identifies ozone (a secondary pollutant) as directly emitted
rubricPoints.exampleEarning: Sulfur dioxide.

parts.label: B
parts.text: Describe how a scrubber reduces pollution from a coal-fired power plant.

rubricPoints.criterion: Describes a scrubber spraying exhaust with a substance such as lime slurry that reacts with and removes sulfur dioxide before it leaves the smokestack.
rubricPoints.exampleEarning: Exhaust passes through a spray of lime slurry that reacts with SO₂ and removes it.

parts.label: C
parts.text: Explain how reducing the household’s electricity purchases could reduce acid deposition.

rubricPoints.criterion: Explains that less coal is burned, so less SO₂ and NOₓ are emitted to form sulfuric and nitric acid in the atmosphere.
commonErrors: says less CO₂ causes less acid rain
rubricPoints.exampleEarning: Less coal burned means less SO₂ and NOₓ, the gases that form sulfuric and nitric acid.

parts.label: D
parts.text: Calculate the percent change in the electricity the household buys from the utility after installing the panels. Show your work.

rubricPoints.criterion: Sets up the calculation with the new purchase of 3,240 kWh: (3,240 − 10,800) / 10,800 × 100.
Calculates a 70% decrease (−70%).
rubricPoints.exampleEarning: −70% (a 70% decrease).

parts.label: E
parts.text: Calculate the mass of CO₂, in kilograms, the household avoids each year. Show your work.

rubricPoints.criterion: Sets up 7,560 kWh × 1.0 kg CO₂/kWh.
rubricPoints.exampleEarning: 7,560 kWh × 1.0 kg/kWh

rubricPoints.criterion: Calculates 7,560 kg of CO₂ per year.
rubricPoints.exampleEarning: 7,560 kg CO₂ per year.

parts.label: F
parts.text: Propose a realistic action, other than installing solar panels, the household could take to reduce its electricity use.

rubricPoints.criterion: Proposes a realistic conservation action such as switching to LED bulbs, buying energy-efficient appliances, adding insulation, or adjusting the thermostat.
rubricPoints.exampleEarning: Replace old appliances with ENERGY STAR models.

parts.label: G
parts.text: Calculate the number of years it will take for the electricity savings to pay for the panels. Show your work.

rubricPoints.criterion: Sets up annual savings (7,560 kWh × $0.14 = $1,058.40) and divides the cost by the savings.
Calculates about 17.9 years (accept 18).

sampleResponse: A Sulfur dioxide. B A scrubber sprays the exhaust with lime slurry, which reacts with sulfur dioxide and removes it before the gas leaves the stack. C Buying less electricity means less coal is burned, so less SO₂ and NOₓ are released to form sulfuric and nitric acid. D The household now buys 10,800 − 7,560 = 3,240 kWh; (3,240 − 10,800) / 10,800 × 100 = −70%. E 7,560 kWh × 1.0 kg/kWh = 7,560 kg CO₂ per year. F Replace incandescent bulbs with LEDs. G Savings = 7,560 × $0.14 = $1,058.40 per year; $18,900 ÷ $1,058.40 ≈ 17.9 years.

title: Invasive Earthworms and Leaf Litter
topic: Soil ecosystems · Invasive species and experimental design

modeledOn.label: 2026 AP Environmental Science Question 1 (Design an Investigation)

stimulus.content:
Figure 1: Bar graph of leaf mass remaining after 12 months: 14.2 grams in plots without earthworms and 5.6 grams in plots with earthworms, from 20.0 grams at the start

Figure 2
Plot type | Native tree seedlings per m²
No earthworms | 18
Earthworms | 6

prompt: Northern hardwood forests developed without earthworms after the last ice age, and their soils are covered by a thick layer of leaf litter. Nonnative earthworms, spread by anglers who discard bait, are now invading these forests. Researchers placed mesh bags containing 20.0 g of dry maple leaves on plots with and without invasive earthworms and measured the mass remaining after 12 months (Figure 1). They also counted native tree seedlings per square meter (Figure 2).

figures.alt: Bar graph of leaf mass remaining after 12 months: 14.2 grams in plots without earthworms and 5.6 grams in plots with earthworms, from 20.0 grams at the start
figures.caption: Figure 1
Figure 2
figures.alt: Figure 2: Plot type No earthworms, Native tree seedlings per m² 18; Plot type Earthworms, Native tree seedlings per m² 6

parts.label: A
parts.text: Describe one characteristic that makes a species likely to become invasive.

rubricPoints.criterion: Describes a trait such as rapid reproduction, generalist diet, tolerance of many conditions, or lack of natural predators in the new range.
rubricPoints.exampleEarning: They reproduce quickly and have no natural predators in the new forest.

parts.label: B
parts.text: Explain how earthworms speed the cycling of nutrients in the forest.

rubricPoints.criterion: Explains that earthworms consume and break down leaf litter, releasing its nutrients into the soil faster.
commonErrors: says earthworms add nutrients from outside the ecosystem
rubricPoints.exampleEarning: They eat the litter and break it into smaller pieces, releasing nitrogen and other nutrients into the soil sooner.

parts.label: C
parts.text: Based on Figure 1, calculate the mass of leaves lost in the earthworm plots.

rubricPoints.criterion: Calculates 14.4 g lost (20.0 − 5.6).

parts.label: D
parts.text: Based on Figure 2, describe the difference in seedling density between the plot types.

rubricPoints.criterion: Describes that plots with earthworms have fewer seedlings (6 versus 18 per m², one-third as many).
rubricPoints.exampleEarning: Earthworm plots have 6 seedlings per m², a third of the 18 in plots without earthworms.

parts.label: E
parts.text: Researchers hypothesized that earthworms reduce seedling survival by removing the leaf litter layer. Describe one way the data support this hypothesis.

rubricPoints.criterion: Connects the two figures: the plots where more litter disappeared (earthworm plots) also had far fewer seedlings.
rubricPoints.exampleEarning: Where earthworms removed most of the litter, seedling density was much lower.

parts.label: F
parts.text: (i) Identify the independent variable in the leaf-bag experiment. (ii) Identify one variable that should be held constant.

rubricPoints.criterion: Identifies the presence or absence of earthworms.
rubricPoints.exampleEarning: Whether earthworms were present.

rubricPoints.criterion: Identifies a valid controlled variable, such as starting leaf mass, leaf species, bag mesh size, length of time, or soil type.
rubricPoints.exampleEarning: The starting mass of leaves in each bag (20.0 g).

parts.label: G
parts.text: (i) Explain why the researchers used several plots of each type rather than one. (ii) Explain how the results might differ if the bags had mesh too small for earthworms to enter.

rubricPoints.criterion: Explains that replication reduces the effect of chance differences between plots and makes results more reliable.
rubricPoints.exampleEarning: Using several plots reduces the chance that one unusual plot skews the results.

rubricPoints.criterion: Explains that if earthworms could not reach the leaves, mass loss in earthworm plots would be closer to the no-earthworm plots, hiding the effect.
commonErrors: says the results would not change
rubricPoints.exampleEarning: Without earthworm access, both plot types would lose similar mass, so the earthworm effect would not show.

parts.label: H
parts.text: Describe one realistic action that could slow the spread of invasive earthworms into new forests.

rubricPoints.criterion: Describes an action such as educating anglers not to dump bait, banning sales of certain bait worms, or cleaning soil from vehicles and equipment.
commonErrors: proposes an action that spreads worms
rubricPoints.exampleEarning: Require bait shops to post signs telling anglers to throw unused worms in the trash.

sampleResponse: A Invasive species often reproduce quickly and have no natural predators in their new range. B Earthworms eat and fragment leaf litter, releasing its nutrients into the soil much faster. C 20.0 − 5.6 = 14.4 g. D Plots with earthworms had 6 seedlings per m², one-third of the 18 per m² without earthworms. E The plots where earthworms removed most of the litter also had far fewer seedlings, consistent with litter loss reducing seedling survival. F (i) Presence or absence of earthworms. (ii) The starting mass of leaves (20.0 g). G (i) Several plots reduce the effect of chance differences between individual plots. (ii) If earthworms could not enter the bags, both plot types would lose similar mass, hiding the earthworm effect. H Educate anglers to discard unused bait worms in the trash instead of on the ground.

figures.alt: Line graph of average depth to the water table: 18 meters in 1980, 26 in 1990, 37 in 2000, 49 in 2010, and 62 in 2020
figures.caption: Figure 1

parts.label: A
parts.text: Based on Figure 1, describe the trend in the depth to the water table from 1980 to 2020.

rubricPoints.criterion: Describes the depth increasing (the water table falling) from about 18 m to 62 m.
rubricPoints.exampleEarning: The depth increased from 18 m to 62 m, so the water table dropped.

parts.label: B
parts.text: Identify the term for withdrawing groundwater faster than it is recharged.

rubricPoints.criterion: Identifies aquifer depletion (overdraft or groundwater mining).
rubricPoints.exampleEarning: Aquifer depletion.

parts.label: C
parts.text: Explain one reason this aquifer recharges very slowly.

rubricPoints.criterion: Explains a reason such as low rainfall in the region, impermeable layers above the aquifer, or water taking a long time to percolate through deep soil and rock.
commonErrors: says the aquifer is too large
rubricPoints.exampleEarning: The region gets little rain, and water must percolate slowly through thick layers of soil and rock.

parts.label: D
parts.text: Describe one environmental consequence of a falling water table, other than reduced water for farms.

rubricPoints.criterion: Describes a consequence such as land subsidence, streams and wetlands drying up, saltwater intrusion near coasts, or wells going dry.
commonErrors: describes a consequence of surface flooding
rubricPoints.exampleEarning: Springs and streams fed by groundwater dry up, harming aquatic habitat.

parts.label: E
parts.text: Propose a realistic solution farmers could implement to reduce groundwater withdrawals.

rubricPoints.criterion: Proposes a realistic solution such as drip irrigation, switching to less water-intensive crops, irrigation scheduling with soil-moisture sensors, or xeriscaping.
rubricPoints.exampleEarning: Switch from center-pivot sprinklers to drip irrigation.

parts.label: F
parts.text: Justify the solution in part E by describing an additional benefit other than conserving water.

rubricPoints.criterion: Describes an additional benefit consistent with part E, such as reduced salinization, lower pumping energy costs, less fertilizer runoff, or higher crop yields.
rubricPoints.exampleEarning: Drip irrigation applies less water to the surface, reducing salt buildup in the soil.

parts.label: G
parts.text: Explain how irrigation in a dry climate can lead to soil salinization.

rubricPoints.criterion: Explains that irrigation water contains dissolved salts; as water evaporates in the hot, dry climate, the salts are left behind and accumulate in the soil.
commonErrors: says salt is added as fertilizer
rubricPoints.exampleEarning: Irrigation water carries small amounts of salt; evaporation leaves the salt in the soil, where it builds up over time.

parts.label: H
parts.text: Identify one crop or diet change that would reduce water use in agriculture.

rubricPoints.criterion: Identifies growing drought-tolerant crops (such as sorghum instead of corn) or eating less meat, especially beef.
rubricPoints.exampleEarning: Grow sorghum instead of corn.

parts.label: I
parts.text: Describe one way that pumping groundwater uses energy and contributes to air pollution.

rubricPoints.criterion: Describes that pumps run on electricity or diesel, and a deeper water table requires more energy, often from fossil fuels that release CO₂ and other pollutants.
rubricPoints.exampleEarning: Pumps powered by diesel or coal electricity must lift water farther as the table drops, burning more fuel.

parts.label: J
parts.text: Describe one policy approach a state government could use to manage the aquifer sustainably.

rubricPoints.criterion: Describes a policy such as pumping limits or permits, metering and pricing groundwater, or subsidies for efficient irrigation.
commonErrors: describes an action individuals take with no policy
rubricPoints.exampleEarning: Require meters on wells and set annual pumping limits for each farm.

sampleResponse: A The depth to the water table increased from about 18 m in 1980 to 62 m in 2020, so the water table has been dropping steadily. B Aquifer depletion. C The region receives little rainfall, and recharge water must percolate slowly through thick soil and rock layers. D Groundwater-fed streams and wetlands dry up, harming aquatic habitats. E Switch to drip irrigation. F Drip irrigation reduces soil salinization because less water evaporates from the surface. G Irrigation water contains dissolved salts; in a dry climate the water evaporates and the salts accumulate in the soil. H Grow drought-tolerant sorghum instead of corn. I Pumps run on diesel or fossil-fuel electricity, and as the water table drops they need more energy, releasing more CO₂. J Require meters on wells and set pumping limits for each farm.

title: A City’s Landfill

modeledOn.type: Analyze an Environmental Problem and Propose a Solution (Doing Calculations)
modeledOn.label: 2026 AP Environmental Science Question 3 (Analyze an Environmental Problem and Propose a Solution (Doing Calculations))

prompt: A city of 120,000 people generates 2.1 kg of municipal solid waste per person per day. All of it currently goes to a landfill with 1,200,000 metric tons of remaining capacity (1 metric ton = 1,000 kg). The city is considering a recycling and composting program that would divert 35% of its waste from the landfill.

parts.label: A
parts.text: Identify the gas produced by anaerobic decomposition in landfills that is a potent greenhouse gas.

rubricPoints.criterion: Identifies methane (CH₄).
rubricPoints.exampleEarning: Methane.

parts.label: B
parts.text: Describe one feature of a modern sanitary landfill that protects groundwater.

rubricPoints.criterion: Describes a feature such as a clay or plastic liner, or a leachate collection system that prevents leachate from reaching groundwater.
commonErrors: describes a feature unrelated to groundwater
rubricPoints.exampleEarning: A clay and plastic liner with pipes that collect leachate for treatment.

parts.label: C
parts.text: Explain why composting food waste reduces methane emissions compared with landfilling it.

rubricPoints.criterion: Explains that composting is aerobic decomposition, which produces CO₂ rather than methane, while buried landfill waste decomposes anaerobically.
rubricPoints.exampleEarning: Compost piles are aerated, so microbes break down food aerobically and produce CO₂ instead of methane.

parts.label: D
parts.text: Calculate the mass of waste, in metric tons, the city sends to the landfill each year without the program. Show your work.

rubricPoints.criterion: Sets up 120,000 people × 2.1 kg/person/day × 365 days ÷ 1,000 kg/t.
commonErrors: forgets to convert kg to t

rubricPoints.criterion: Calculates 91,980 metric tons per year (accept about 92,000).
rubricPoints.exampleEarning: 91,980 t per year.

parts.label: E
parts.text: Calculate the mass of waste, in metric tons per year, that the program would divert. Show your work.

rubricPoints.criterion: Sets up 0.35 × (the annual total from part D).
Calculates about 32,193 t per year (accept 32,000), consistent with part D.
rubricPoints.exampleEarning: 32,193 t per year.

parts.label: F
parts.text: Propose a realistic action, other than recycling and composting, that would reduce the amount of waste the city generates.

rubricPoints.criterion: Proposes source reduction, such as a pay-as-you-throw fee, a ban or fee on single-use bags, or encouraging reusable containers.
rubricPoints.exampleEarning: Charge households per bag of trash (pay-as-you-throw).

parts.label: G
parts.text: Calculate how many more years the landfill will last with the program than without it. Show your work.

rubricPoints.criterion: Sets up the lifetimes: 1,200,000 ÷ 91,980 and 1,200,000 ÷ (91,980 − 32,193), then subtracts.
Calculates about 7.0 more years (20.1 − 13.0).

sampleResponse: A Methane. B A clay and plastic liner with a leachate collection system keeps leachate out of groundwater. C Composting is aerobic, so microbes produce CO₂ rather than the methane formed when buried waste decomposes anaerobically. D 120,000 × 2.1 kg × 365 = 91,980,000 kg = 91,980 t per year. E 0.35 × 91,980 = 32,193 t per year. F Charge households per bag of trash (pay-as-you-throw). G Without the program: 1,200,000 ÷ 91,980 ≈ 13.0 years. With it: 1,200,000 ÷ 59,787 ≈ 20.1 years. The landfill lasts about 7.0 more years.
